```{r}
  skew      <- two_tp_shapiro_df$Skewness[two_tp_shapiro_df$DiffCol == diff_col]
  kurt      <- two_tp_shapiro_df$Excess_Kurtosis[two_tp_shapiro_df$DiffCol == diff_col]

  skew_kurt_in_range <- (skew >= -1 && skew <= 1) && (kurt >= -2 && kurt <= 2)

  if (shapiro_p > 0.05) {
    use_ttest      <- TRUE
    decision_basis <- "Shapiro-Wilk normal (p > .05)"
  } else if (skew_kurt_in_range) {
    use_ttest      <- TRUE
    decision_basis <- "Shapiro-Wilk significant, but skew/kurtosis in range — treated as normal"
  } else {
    use_ttest      <- FALSE
    decision_basis <- "Shapiro-Wilk significant, skew/kurtosis outside range — non-normal"
  }

  two_tp_test_recommendations <- rbind(two_tp_test_recommendations, data.frame(
    Measure           = label,
    Use_TTest         = use_ttest,
    Recommended_Test  = if (use_ttest) "Paired t-test" else "Wilcoxon Signed-Rank",
    Decision_Basis    = decision_basis,
    stringsAsFactors  = FALSE
  ))
}

print(two_tp_test_recommendations)

if (interactive()) {

  cat("\nRecommended tests are shown above, based on Shapiro-Wilk, skewness, and kurtosis for each measure's difference score.\n")
  cat("Before continuing: scroll back and check the Q-Q plots and normality histograms above for each measure, especially any row where Decision_Basis mentions an override or a non-normal result.\n\n")

  response <- readline(prompt = "Happy with the recommended tests above? Continue with these? (y/n): ")
  if (!tolower(trimws(response)) %in% c("y", "yes")) {
    stop("Stopped for test-selection review. Re-run this chunk and answer 'y' once you've checked the Q-Q plots and histograms above, or reconsider the skew/kurtosis override thresholds first if a recommendation looks wrong.")
  }
  print("Continuing — recommended tests reviewed and accepted.")

} else {
  stop("This chunk requires interactive confirmation of the recommended tests before continuing. Rendering stops here — run this chunk yourself in the console first, review the Q-Q plots and histograms above, and confirm before rendering the full document.")
}
```

### Run confirmed tests and compute effect sizes

::: callout-note
**Wilcoxon effect size.** The effect size on Wilcoxon rows is the rank-biserial correlation from `effectsize::rank_biserial()` (Kerby, 2014). Reversing which timepoint is first flips its sign and keeps its magnitude.
:::

::: callout-note
**Effect size reporting.** `Effect_Size` and `Effect_Type` report whichever effect size the row's own test produces: Cohen's *d* from `effectsize::cohens_d()` on a t-test row, rank-biserial *r* from `effectsize::rank_biserial()` on a Wilcoxon row. There is no separate always-populated Cohen's *d* column. Because *d* and *r* are on different scales, effect magnitudes cannot be compared directly between t-test and Wilcoxon rows.
:::

::: callout-note
**No confidence interval on `Effect_Size`.** Both effect size functions are called with `ci = NULL`, and confidence intervals are reported for the mean difference only. Because `Mean_Diff_CI` is also `NA` on Wilcoxon rows (see below), a Wilcoxon row carries a point estimate and a p-value with no interval.
:::

::: callout-note
**`DF` and `Mean_Diff_CI_Lower`/`Upper` are `NA` on Wilcoxon rows, deliberately.** A Wilcoxon signed-rank test doesn't estimate a parametric mean difference or have a *t*-distribution degrees-of-freedom — it tests a rank-based location shift. Rather than putting a number there that would misrepresent what the test actually estimated, both columns are left blank on those rows.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-two-tp-statistical-tests
# Formats a numeric p-value for display: anything below .001 shows as
# "<0.001" rather than rounding to a misleading 0. Defined once here so
# the identical rule applies to both the raw and Bonferroni-adjusted
# p-value columns below, rather than writing the same logic out twice.
# Rounds to a fixed 3 decimal places with sprintf("%.3f", ...) and not to 3
# significant figures, because signif() lets some values through with 4 decimal
# places (e.g. 0.0238 stays "0.0238"), which gives inconsistent precision across
# measures on the same figure. sprintf() also keeps trailing zeros
# (0.5 -> "0.500"), matching APA-style p-value reporting.
format_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
}

# Saved copy of this function under its own name. Part 3 defines its own
# format_p() later (with a space: "< 0.001"), which would overwrite this one.
# The two-timepoint p-values are formatted in Part 3 (after the correction by
# hypothesis group), and stage 6 checks them against the no-space "<0.001",
# so they must keep using this version.
format_p_two_tp <- format_p

two_tp_test_results <- list()

two_tp_test_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure            = character(),
  Test               = character(),
  Decision_Basis     = character(),
  N                  = numeric(),
  N_Zero_Change      = numeric(),
  Direction          = character(),
  Mean_TP1           = numeric(),
  SD_TP1             = numeric(),
  Median_TP1         = numeric(),
  Mean_TP5           = numeric(),
  SD_TP5             = numeric(),
  Median_TP5         = numeric(),
  Mean_Difference    = numeric(),
  SEM                = numeric(),
  Statistic          = numeric(),
  Statistic_Type     = character(),
  DF                 = numeric(),
  Mean_Diff_CI_Lower = numeric(),
  Mean_Diff_CI_Upper = numeric(),
  Effect_Size        = numeric(),
  Effect_Type        = character(),
  P_Value_Raw        = numeric(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(two_tp_lookup))) {

  diff_col  <- two_tp_lookup$DiffCol[i]
  pre_col   <- two_tp_lookup$PreCol[i]
  post_col  <- two_tp_lookup$PostCol[i]
  label     <- two_tp_lookup$Label[i]
  direction <- two_tp_lookup$Direction[i]

  pre_vals  <- two_tp_data[[pre_col]]
  post_vals <- two_tp_data[[post_col]]
  diff_vals <- two_tp_data[[diff_col]]

  n_pairs   <- sum(!is.na(diff_vals))

  # How many complete pairs had TP5 - TP1 = 0 exactly. These are the cases
  # the Wilcoxon signed-rank test drops before ranking (it ranks non-zero
  # differences only), so this number is what "N" doesn't tell you on its
  # own: how many of the N pairs actually informed the test result versus
  # sat out as ties. Computed for every measure regardless of route, not
  # just Wilcoxon ones, so t-test-route measures have it on hand too if
  # ever wanted (see callout below on why it isn't currently surfaced in
  # the t-test split table).
  n_zero_diff <- sum(diff_vals == 0, na.rm = TRUE)

  mean_pre    <- mean(pre_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_pre      <- sd(pre_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  median_pre  <- median(pre_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean_post   <- mean(post_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  sd_post     <- sd(post_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  median_post <- median(post_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean_diff   <- mean(diff_vals, na.rm = TRUE)
  sem         <- sd(diff_vals, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n_pairs)

  # Pulls the confirmed recommendation from the human-in-the-loop chunk
  # above, rather than recalculating the decision here — one source of
  # truth for which test each measure actually runs.
  rec            <- two_tp_test_recommendations[two_tp_test_recommendations$Measure == label, ]
  use_ttest      <- rec$Use_TTest
  decision_basis <- rec$Decision_Basis

  if (use_ttest) {
    # post_vals first — t.test(pre, post) would compute its statistic as
    # (pre - post), the opposite sign to Mean_Difference elsewhere in this
    # same row. post_vals first keeps every figure in a t-test row pointed
    # the same direction.
    res                <- t.test(post_vals, pre_vals, paired = TRUE)
    test_name          <- "Paired t-test"
    statistic          <- res$statistic
    statistic_type     <- "t"
    df                 <- res$parameter
    mean_diff_ci_lower <- res$conf.int[1]
    mean_diff_ci_upper <- res$conf.int[2]

    d_res       <- as.data.frame(cohens_d(post_vals, pre_vals, paired = TRUE, ci = NULL))
    effect_size <- d_res$Cohens_d
    effect_type <- "d"

  } else {
    res                <- wilcox.test(pre_vals, post_vals, paired = TRUE)
    test_name          <- "Wilcoxon Signed-Rank"
    statistic          <- res$statistic
    statistic_type     <- "W"
    df                 <- NA_real_
    mean_diff_ci_lower <- NA_real_
    mean_diff_ci_upper <- NA_real_

    rb_res      <- as.data.frame(rank_biserial(post_vals, pre_vals, paired = TRUE, ci = NULL))
    effect_size <- rb_res$r_rank_biserial
    effect_type <- "r"
  }

  two_tp_test_results[[label]] <- res

  two_tp_test_summary <- rbind(two_tp_test_summary, data.frame(
    Measure            = label,
    Test               = test_name,
    Decision_Basis     = decision_basis,
    N                  = n_pairs,
    N_Zero_Change      = n_zero_diff,
    Direction          = direction,
    Mean_TP1           = round(mean_pre, 3),
    SD_TP1             = round(sd_pre, 3),
    Median_TP1         = round(median_pre, 3),
    Mean_TP5           = round(mean_post, 3),
    SD_TP5             = round(sd_post, 3),
    Median_TP5         = round(median_post, 3),
    Mean_Difference    = round(mean_diff, 3),
    SEM                = round(sem, 3),
    Statistic          = round(statistic, 3),
    Statistic_Type     = statistic_type,
    DF                 = df,
    Mean_Diff_CI_Lower = round(mean_diff_ci_lower, 3),
    Mean_Diff_CI_Upper = round(mean_diff_ci_upper, 3),
    Effect_Size        = round(effect_size, 3),
    Effect_Type        = effect_type,
    P_Value_Raw        = res$p.value,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

# The Bonferroni correction is not applied here. It runs once in Part 3, across
# each hypothesis group (Mental health, Wellbeing, Behaviour, Workplace
# performance), because a group's family combines these two-timepoint tests with
# the three-timepoint post-hoc comparisons, which do not exist yet at this point.
# P_Value_Raw stays as an unrounded number here. The corrected columns, the
# display formatting and the split tables (two_tp_ttest, two_tp_wilcoxon) are
# all produced in Part 3.

cat("Raw (uncorrected) p-values only. Correction by hypothesis group is applied in Part 3.\n")
print(two_tp_test_summary)
```

::: callout-note
**Two-timepoint output tables.** `two_tp_test_summary` is the single computed table and is what `s05-save-handoff` passes to stage 6. `two_tp_ttest` and `two_tp_wilcoxon` are display-only copies, filtered and renamed after the Bonferroni correction so each shows only the quantities its test reports. The correction is not run separately on them. `two_tp_wilcoxon` mirrors `posthoc_wilcoxon` as far as this route allows: `Median_TP1` and `Median_TP5` replace the means, and `V` and `Rank_Biserial_r` replace the generic `Statistic` and `Effect_Size`. There is no `Comparison` column, because every row here is TP1 vs TP5. `Decision_Basis` is kept in both tables and records whether a measure took the t-test route through plain normality or through the skewness and kurtosis override.

`Median_TP1` and `Median_TP5` are computed inside the main loop (`s05-two-tp-statistical-tests`), rounded to 3 decimal places like the other figures in that table.

**`N_Zero_Change`.** A Wilcoxon signed-rank test ranks only the non-zero differences, so pairs where TP5 minus TP1 is exactly 0 are dropped before ranking. For a floor-effected measure such as Days Surfing per Month, `N` alone can make the test look like it covers the whole sample. `N_Zero_Change` (`sum(diff_vals == 0, na.rm = TRUE)`) shows how many pairs were dropped, so `N = 59, N_Zero_Change = 49` means only 10 pairs contributed to the test. It is computed for every measure and stored in `two_tp_test_summary`, but shown only in `two_tp_wilcoxon`, because a paired t-test does not drop zero-difference pairs.
:::

The two split tables described above (`two_tp_ttest`, `two_tp_wilcoxon`) are built at the end of Part 3, not here. They need the Bonferroni-corrected p-values, and the correction runs across each hypothesis group, combining these tests with the Part 3 post-hoc comparisons (see the callout in Part 3).

## Part 3 — Three-timepoint measures (TP1/TP4/TP5)

SWEMWBS, PHQ-8, GAD-7, MHSIS, BRS, UWES, OSES, BAT Total + 4 subscales, GSPA, and Intention to Leave. All have data at all three timepoints, so these go through repeated-measures ANOVA (or Friedman, if assumptions aren't met), not the paired-difference route above.

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-measure-list
three_tp_measures <- tribble(
  ~Label,                       ~TP1_col,                  ~TP4_col,                  ~TP5_col,                   ~Direction,
  "SWEMWBS Metric",             "SWEMWBS_Metric_TP1",      "SWEMWBS_Metric_TP4",      "SWEMWBS_Metric_TP5",       "Higher = Improvement",
  "PHQ-8 Total",                "PHQ8_Total_TP1",          "PHQ8_Total_TP4",          "PHQ8_Total_TP5",           "Lower = Improvement",
  "GAD-7 Total",                "GAD7_Total_TP1",          "GAD7_Total_TP4",          "GAD7_Total_TP5",           "Lower = Improvement",
  "MHSIS Mean",                 "MHSIS_Mean_TP1",          "MHSIS_Mean_TP4",          "MHSIS_Mean_TP5",           "Higher = Improvement",
  "BRS Mean",                   "BRS_Mean_TP1",            "BRS_Mean_TP4",            "BRS_Mean_TP5",             "Higher = Improvement",
  "UWES Total",                 "UWES_Total_TP1",          "UWES_Total_TP4",          "UWES_Total_TP5",           "Higher = Improvement",
  "OSES Total",                 "OSES_Total_TP1",          "OSES_Total_TP4",          "OSES_Total_TP5",           "Higher = Improvement",
  "BAT Total Mean",             "BAT_TotalMean_TP1",       "BAT_TotalMean_TP4",       "BAT_TotalMean_TP5",        "Lower = Improvement",
  "BAT Exhaustion",             "BAT_Exhaustion_TP1",      "BAT_Exhaustion_TP4",      "BAT_Exhaustion_TP5",       "Lower = Improvement",
  "BAT Mental Distance",        "BAT_MentalDistance_TP1",  "BAT_MentalDistance_TP4",  "BAT_MentalDistance_TP5",   "Lower = Improvement",
  "BAT Emotional Impairment",   "BAT_EmoImpairment_TP1",   "BAT_EmoImpairment_TP4",   "BAT_EmoImpairment_TP5",    "Lower = Improvement",
  "BAT Cognitive Impairment",   "BAT_CogImpairment_TP1",   "BAT_CogImpairment_TP4",   "BAT_CogImpairment_TP5",    "Lower = Improvement",
  "GSPA Total",                 "GSPA_Total_TP1",          "GSPA_Total_TP4",          "GSPA_Total_TP5",           "Higher = Improvement",
  "INTL Total",                 "INTL_Total_TP1",          "INTL_Total_TP4",          "INTL_Total_TP5",           "Lower = Improvement"
)
```

### Reshape to long format

RM-ANOVA and Friedman both need one row per person per timepoint (long format), not one row per person with three columns (wide format) — this is what `rstatix`'s functions expect. Each measure gets its own long-format data frame, kept in a named list (`three_tp_long`) so later steps can loop over them.

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-reshape-long
make_long <- function(label, tp1_col, tp4_col, tp5_col) {
  scored_data |>
    select(ID, all_of(c(tp1_col, tp4_col, tp5_col))) |>
    pivot_longer(
      cols      = -ID,
      names_to  = "Timepoint",
      values_to = "Score"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Timepoint = case_when(
        Timepoint == tp1_col ~ "TP1",
        Timepoint == tp4_col ~ "TP4",
        Timepoint == tp5_col ~ "TP5"
      ),
      Timepoint = factor(Timepoint, levels = c("TP1", "TP4", "TP5"))
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(Score))
}

three_tp_long <- pmap(
  list(three_tp_measures$Label, three_tp_measures$TP1_col, three_tp_measures$TP4_col, three_tp_measures$TP5_col),
  make_long
)
names(three_tp_long) <- three_tp_measures$Label
```

### Sample definition: complete cases only

RM-ANOVA and Friedman both need a score at *all three* timepoints per person — a person with only TP1 and TP4 can't contribute to either test. This keeps only IDs with all three timepoints present, per measure, and reports how many people that leaves compared to how many had at least some data.

::: callout-warning
**Duplicate check.** The filter checks that each retained person has exactly one row at each of TP1, TP4 and TP5, and not merely three rows in total. `friedman_test()` needs one observation per person per timepoint and errors with "not an unreplicated complete block design" otherwise. If duplicates are reported, the cause is most likely upstream (probably the merge in stage 2), so trace it back to source and do not simply drop the duplicate here, because a duplicated participant row could also inflate the sample size elsewhere.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-complete-cases
# Diagnostic: flag any (Measure, ID, Timepoint) combination with more than
# one row, *before* filtering anything out, so duplicates are visible rather
# than silently dropped or silently causing a downstream crash.
three_tp_duplicate_check <- map_dfr(names(three_tp_long), function(label) {
  three_tp_long[[label]] |>
    count(ID, Timepoint, name = "N_Rows") |>
    filter(N_Rows > 1) |>
    mutate(Measure = label) |>
    relocate(Measure)
})

if (nrow(three_tp_duplicate_check) > 0) {
  print("⚠️ Duplicate ID/Timepoint rows found — see three_tp_duplicate_check for exactly which IDs and measures are affected. This is very likely a data issue upstream (check stage 2, the rename and merge, for a many-to-many merge), not something to silently fix here.")
  print(three_tp_duplicate_check)
} else {
  print("✅ No duplicate ID/Timepoint rows found in any measure.")
}

# Complete-case filter: requires exactly one row at each of TP1, TP4, TP5 —
# not just 3 rows in total, which would not rule out duplicates.
three_tp_long <- map(three_tp_long, function(df) {
  ids_complete <- df |>
    distinct(ID, Timepoint) |>
    count(ID) |>
    filter(n == 3) |>
    pull(ID)

  df |>
    filter(ID %in% ids_complete) |>
    distinct(ID, Timepoint, .keep_all = TRUE)
})

three_tp_sample_sizes <- map_dfr(names(three_tp_long), function(label) {
  tibble(
    Measure         = label,
    N_Complete_Cases = n_distinct(three_tp_long[[label]]$ID)
  )
})

print(three_tp_sample_sizes)
```

### Outlier detection (raw scores per timepoint)

Outliers are checked on raw scores at each timepoint separately, using `rstatix::identify_outliers()`, the tool built for this design, and not the difference-score approach used in Part 2. This flags anyone whose score is unusually high or low *at a given timepoint*, and not anyone whose *change* looks unusual.

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-outlier-detection
three_tp_outliers <- map(three_tp_long, function(df) {
  df |>
    group_by(Timepoint) |>
    identify_outliers(Score) |>
    ungroup()
})

any_outliers <- any(map_lgl(three_tp_outliers, ~ nrow(.x) > 0))

if (any_outliers) {
  print("❌ Outliers detected in the following measures (raw scores, per timepoint):")
  for (label in names(three_tp_outliers)) {
    if (nrow(three_tp_outliers[[label]]) > 0) {
      cat("\n---", label, "---\n")
      print(three_tp_outliers[[label]] |> select(ID, Timepoint, Score, is.outlier, is.extreme))
    }
  }

  if (interactive()) {
    response <- readline(prompt = "Outliers detected (see above). Continue anyway? (y/n): ")
    if (!tolower(trimws(response)) %in% c("y", "yes")) {
      stop("Analysis stopped after reviewing outliers. Re-run this chunk and answer 'y' to continue, or address the outliers first.")
    }
    print("Continuing with analysis — outliers were reviewed and accepted.")
  } else {
    stop("Outliers detected — see the table above. Rendering stops here because there is no way to confirm continuation during a non-interactive render. Run this chunk interactively in the console first to review and confirm before rendering the full document.")
  }

} else {
  print("✅ No outliers detected in any measure, at any timepoint.")
}
```

### Normality tests (per timepoint)

Same decision rule as the two-timepoint route (Part 2): if Shapiro-Wilk is non-significant (p \> .05), treat that timepoint as normal. If it **is** significant, check skewness (±1) and excess kurtosis (±2) before accepting that verdict — if both are in range, treat it as normal anyway (Shapiro-Wilk oversensitivity), otherwise it's genuinely non-normal. This runs **separately at TP1, TP4, and TP5** for each measure, since RM-ANOVA's normality assumption is about each timepoint's distribution individually, not one single difference score. A measure only routes to RM-ANOVA if **all three** timepoints pass; if even one timepoint fails (after the skew/kurtosis check), the whole measure routes to Friedman instead.

::: callout-note
**Skewness and kurtosis** use `psych::skew()` and `psych::kurtosi()` with `type = 2`, the same as Part 2, so both routes report the same estimator. This chunk depends only on the `psych` package loaded in `s05-setup`.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-normality-tests
three_tp_shapiro <- map(three_tp_long, function(df) {
  df |>
    group_by(Timepoint) |>
    shapiro_test(Score) |>
    ungroup()
})

three_tp_skew_kurt <- map(three_tp_long, function(df) {
  df |>
    group_by(Timepoint) |>
    summarise(
      Skewness        = round(psych::skew(Score, type = 2, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
      Excess_Kurtosis = round(psych::kurtosi(Score, type = 2, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
})

three_tp_normality_detail <- map_dfr(names(three_tp_shapiro), function(label) {
  shap <- three_tp_shapiro[[label]] |> select(Timepoint, W_Statistic = statistic, P_Value = p)
  sk   <- three_tp_skew_kurt[[label]]
  left_join(shap, sk, by = "Timepoint") |>
    mutate(Measure = label) |>
    relocate(Measure)
}) |>
  mutate(
    Skew_Kurt_In_Range = (Skewness >= -1 & Skewness <= 1) & (Excess_Kurtosis >= -2 & Excess_Kurtosis <= 2),
    Normal = case_when(
      P_Value > 0.05                        ~ TRUE,
      P_Value <= 0.05 & Skew_Kurt_In_Range   ~ TRUE,
      TRUE                                    ~ FALSE
    ),
    Decision_Basis = case_when(
      P_Value > 0.05                        ~ "Shapiro-Wilk normal (p > .05)",
      P_Value <= 0.05 & Skew_Kurt_In_Range   ~ "Shapiro-Wilk significant, but skew/kurtosis in range — treated as normal",
      TRUE                                    ~ "Shapiro-Wilk significant, skew/kurtosis outside range — non-normal"
    )
  )

print(three_tp_normality_detail)

three_tp_shapiro_summary <- three_tp_normality_detail |>
  group_by(Measure) |>
  summarise(All_Normal = all(Normal), .groups = "drop")

print(three_tp_shapiro_summary)
```

### Normality histograms

One histogram per measure per timepoint (three per measure), each showing the Shapiro-Wilk p-value, skewness, excess kurtosis, and which decision path that timepoint took.

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-normality-histograms
#| results: asis

for (label in names(three_tp_long)) {

  df <- three_tp_long[[label]]

  for (tp in c("TP1", "TP4", "TP5")) {

    detail_row <- three_tp_normality_detail |>
      filter(Measure == label, Timepoint == tp)

    if (nrow(detail_row) == 0) next

    plot_data <- df |> filter(Timepoint == tp)

    p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = Score)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
      labs(
        title    = paste0(label, " — ", tp_labels[tp]),
        subtitle = paste0("Shapiro-Wilk p: ", sprintf("%.3f", detail_row$P_Value),
                           "  |  Skewness: ", detail_row$Skewness,
                           "  |  Excess kurtosis: ", detail_row$Excess_Kurtosis,
                           "\n", detail_row$Decision_Basis),
        x        = "Score",
        y        = "Count"
      ) +
      theme_classic()

    print(p)
  }
}
```

### Q-Q plots

::: callout-note
**Q-Q plots** use the same source and substitution as the two-timepoint Q-Q plots above: Field, A., & Field, A. (2026). *Discovering statistics using R & RStudio* (2nd ed.). Sage. (p. 380). Base `ggplot2`'s `stat_qq()` and `stat_qq_line()` replace `qqplotr`, with colours and theme matched to the rest of the pipeline.
:::

One Q-Q plot per measure per timepoint (three per measure, 42 in total), individually rather than faceted together — matching the same per-timepoint structure as the histograms above, so each plot can be checked against its own row in `three_tp_normality_detail`.

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-qq-plots
#| results: asis

for (label in names(three_tp_long)) {

  df <- three_tp_long[[label]]

  for (tp in c("TP1", "TP4", "TP5")) {

    plot_data <- df |> filter(Timepoint == tp)

    if (nrow(plot_data) == 0) next

    p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(sample = Score)) +
      stat_qq(color = "grey40", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.5) +
      stat_qq_line(color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
      labs(
        title = paste0("Q-Q Plot — ", label, " — ", tp_labels[tp]),
        x     = "Theoretical quantiles",
        y     = "Sample quantiles"
      ) +
      theme_classic()

    print(p)
  }
}
```

### Manual normality override

Skewness and excess kurtosis, the two statistics the automated decision above falls back on when Shapiro-Wilk is significant, only detect asymmetry and tail weight. Neither one can detect a multimodal or "gappy" shape — a distribution can be symmetric with normal-ish tails and still look nothing like a bell curve on a histogram. This matters here because several measures in this pipeline have a small number of possible integer values (e.g. INTL Total, a 2-item summed scale with only 7 possible totals), which tends to produce exactly this kind of comb-shaped histogram regardless of the underlying construct — a shape the skew/kurtosis override is blind to. This section exists to let you overrule the automated decision for specific measures, based on what you actually saw in the histograms/Q-Q plots above, with the reason recorded permanently alongside the change.

::: callout-note
**Two-step process, not a single chunk.** Step one below writes an Excel template pre-filled with every measure/timepoint and its automated decision — you never type a measure name, so there's no way to misspell one into a silent no-op. Open the file, fill in `Override_Normal` (`TRUE`/`FALSE`) and `Reason` only for the rows you want to change, leave everything else blank, and save. Step two, a separate chunk, reads the saved file back in and applies whatever you filled in. This can't be one continuous chunk, since it depends on you editing a file outside R in between — same reason the outlier and test-recommendation checks elsewhere in this document use an interactive pause rather than running straight through.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-normality-override-template
override_template_path <- here("data", "analysis", "normality_override_template.xlsx")

# Skips regeneration if the file already exists, so a re-run of this chunk
# (or a full render, once the template has been created and filled in) cannot
# overwrite entries you have already entered, and does not stop the render.
# Delete the file manually first if you want a fresh blank template.
if (file.exists(override_template_path)) {

  print(paste0(
    "Override template already exists at ", override_template_path,
    " — leaving it as-is rather than regenerating it, in case it's already ",
    "been filled in. Delete it manually first if you want a fresh template."
  ))

} else {

  normality_override_template <- three_tp_normality_detail |>
    select(
      Measure, Timepoint,
      Shapiro_Wilk_P     = P_Value,
      Skewness, Excess_Kurtosis,
      Automated_Decision = Normal
    ) |>
    mutate(
      Override_Normal = NA,
      Reason          = NA_character_
    )

  write_xlsx(normality_override_template, path = override_template_path)

  print(paste0(
    "Template written to ", override_template_path,
    " — open it, compare Automated_Decision against the histograms/Q-Q plots above, ",
    "and fill in Override_Normal (TRUE/FALSE) + Reason only for the rows you want to change. ",
    "Leave every other row blank. Save the file, then run the next chunk."
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-normality-override-apply
normality_overrides_filled <- read_excel(override_template_path)

# Blank Override_Normal means "accept the automated decision" — only rows
# where you actually filled something in count as an override.
active_overrides <- normality_overrides_filled |>
  filter(!is.na(Override_Normal))

if (nrow(active_overrides) > 0) {

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(active_overrides))) {
    ov_measure   <- active_overrides$Measure[i]
    ov_timepoint <- active_overrides$Timepoint[i]
    ov_normal    <- as.logical(active_overrides$Override_Normal[i])
    ov_reason    <- active_overrides$Reason[i]

    match_rows <- three_tp_normality_detail$Measure == ov_measure &
      three_tp_normality_detail$Timepoint == ov_timepoint

    three_tp_normality_detail$Normal[match_rows] <- ov_normal
    three_tp_normality_detail$Decision_Basis[match_rows] <- paste0(
      "Manually overridden to ", ifelse(ov_normal, "normal", "non-normal"),
      " — ", ov_reason
    )
  }

  print("Overrides applied:")
  print(active_overrides |> select(Measure, Timepoint, Override_Normal, Reason))

} else {
  print("No overrides found in the template — every measure/timepoint keeps its automated decision.")
}

# Recomputed from the (possibly overridden) per-timepoint Normal column,
# same logic as before the override step existed — this stays the single
# source of truth the routing block below reads from, whether or not any
# override was actually applied above.
three_tp_shapiro_summary <- three_tp_normality_detail |>
  group_by(Measure) |>
  summarise(All_Normal = all(Normal), .groups = "drop")

print(three_tp_shapiro_summary)
```

### RM-ANOVA / Friedman route decision, tests, and post-hoc

For each measure: if all three timepoints passed normality, run RM-ANOVA (`rstatix::anova_test()`, which applies the Greenhouse-Geisser correction automatically when Mauchly's test says sphericity is violated, and reports generalised eta-squared as `ges`) followed by Bonferroni-corrected pairwise paired t-tests. If not, run a Friedman test (with Kendall's *W* as its effect size) followed by Bonferroni-corrected pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests instead. Either way, Cohen's *d* is computed for every pairwise comparison and reported alongside the test's own effect size, same convention as Part 2.

::: callout-note
**Why `rstatix::anova_test()` and not `afex`.** Both packages would give the same underlying statistics here — same Greenhouse-Geisser correction, same sphericity handling. `rstatix` was chosen because every function takes a tidy data frame and returns a tidy data frame, matching the rest of this pipeline, rather than `afex`'s model-object-then-extract workflow. The one thing this means being deliberate about: `rstatix::anova_test()` reports generalised eta-squared (`ges`) by default, which is the effect size actually recommended for repeated-measures designs (it stays comparable across studies with different numbers of within-subject levels) — so no extra step is needed to request it, but it's worth knowing that's what the `ges` column means if you're writing this up.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-three-tp-anova-friedman-posthoc
omnibus_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure        = character(),
  Test           = character(),
  N              = numeric(),
  Direction      = character(),
  Statistic      = numeric(),
  Statistic_Type = character(),
  DFn            = numeric(),
  DFd            = numeric(),
  Effect_Size    = numeric(),
  Effect_Type    = character(),
  P_Value        = character(),
  Sphericity_Correction = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# format_p() keeps the leading zero (e.g. "0.043", not ".043"), a deliberate
# departure from strict APA style, which drops it for any statistic that cannot
# exceed 1. It writes "< 0.001" with a space, so a sentence reads "p < 0.001"
# and not "p <0.001". It rounds to a fixed 3 decimal places with
# sprintf("%.3f", ...), the same as the two-timepoint format_p(), because
# signif(p, 3) gives inconsistent precision across measures (0.0238 stays
# "0.0238"). sprintf() also keeps trailing zeros, matching APA convention.
format_p <- function(p) {
  ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))
}

# APA-style degrees-of-freedom formatting: whole numbers print as whole
# numbers (F(2, 58)); fractional values — which only happen when
# Greenhouse-Geisser correction has fired — print to 2 decimal places
# (F(1.03, 30.01)), since the fractional df is itself part of how a
# reader recognises a corrected result.
format_df <- function(x) {
  ifelse(abs(x - round(x)) < 1e-8, as.character(round(x)), sprintf("%.2f", x))
}

# Builds the "p = 0.XXX" / "p < 0.001" clause from an already-formatted
# p-value string (i.e. after format_p() has run on it).
apa_p_clause <- function(p_formatted) {
  ifelse(startsWith(p_formatted, "<"), paste("p", p_formatted), paste0("p = ", p_formatted))
}

omnibus_sentences <- data.frame(
  Measure  = character(),
  Sentence = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

posthoc_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure       = character(),
  Comparison    = character(),
  N             = numeric(),
  N_Zero_Change = numeric(),
  Direction     = character(),
  Mean_Group1   = numeric(),
  Mean_Group2   = numeric(),
  Median_Group1 = numeric(),
  Median_Group2 = numeric(),
  Mean_Diff     = numeric(),
  SE            = numeric(),
  Statistic     = numeric(),
  Statistic_Type = character(),
  Effect_Size   = numeric(),
  Effect_Type   = character(),
  P_Value_Raw   = numeric(),
  Group1        = character(),
  Group2        = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (label in three_tp_measures$Label) {

  df        <- three_tp_long[[label]]
  is_normal <- three_tp_shapiro_summary$All_Normal[three_tp_shapiro_summary$Measure == label]
  direction <- three_tp_measures$Direction[three_tp_measures$Label == label]
  n_pairs   <- n_distinct(df$ID)

  group_means <- df |>
    group_by(Timepoint) |>
    summarise(Mean = mean(Score, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

  # Wide format, one row per participant — needed below for Mean_Diff/SE,
  # medians, rank_biserial(), and the per-row Cohen's d, all of which take
  # matched-pair numeric vectors directly rather than a formula.
  df_wide <- df |>
    select(ID, Timepoint, Score) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Timepoint, values_from = Score)

  if (is_normal) {

    ## RM-ANOVA route -----------------------------------------------------
    aov_res   <- anova_test(data = df, dv = Score, wid = ID, within = Timepoint)
    aov_table <- get_anova_table(aov_res, correction = "auto")

    omnibus_p <- aov_table$p
    p_display <- format_p(omnibus_p)

    # get_anova_table(correction = "auto") checks Mauchly's test itself and
    # applies Greenhouse-Geisser correction to the DFn/DFd/F/p values above
    # whenever sphericity is violated (Mauchly's p < .05) — it does this
    # silently, without a separate flag in its output, so this note records
    # the same rule rather than trying to read a flag back out of the object.
    mauchly_p <- aov_res$`Mauchly's Test for Sphericity`$p
    correction_used <- if (!is.null(mauchly_p) && mauchly_p < 0.05) {
      paste0("Applied (Mauchly's p = ", signif(mauchly_p, 3), " < .05)")
    } else if (!is.null(mauchly_p)) {
      paste0("Not needed (Mauchly's p = ", signif(mauchly_p, 3), " >= .05)")
    } else {
      "Mauchly's test not returned — check aov_res manually"
    }

    omnibus_summary <- rbind(omnibus_summary, data.frame(
      Measure        = label,
      Test           = "RM-ANOVA",
      N              = n_pairs,
      Direction      = direction,
      Statistic      = round(aov_table$F, 3),
      Statistic_Type = "F",
      DFn            = aov_table$DFn,
      DFd            = aov_table$DFd,
      Effect_Size    = round(aov_table$ges, 3),
      Effect_Type    = "ges",
      P_Value        = p_display,
      Sphericity_Correction = correction_used,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))

    # APA sentence built here, while the raw numeric values are still in
    # scope — omnibus tests aren't Bonferroni-corrected (a separate, still
    # -open question), so unlike the post-hoc sentences below, this one
    # doesn't need to wait for anything computed after the loop.
    gg_clause  <- if (grepl("^Applied", correction_used)) " with a Greenhouse-Geisser correction" else ""
    sig_clause <- if (omnibus_p < 0.05) {
      "revealed a statistically significant effect of time on"
    } else {
      "did not reveal a statistically significant effect of time on"
    }
    omnibus_sentence <- paste0(
      "A repeated measures ANOVA", gg_clause, " ", sig_clause, " ", label,
      ", F(", format_df(aov_table$DFn), ", ", format_df(aov_table$DFd), ") = ",
      sprintf("%.2f", aov_table$F), ", ", apa_p_clause(p_display), ", ges = ",
      sprintf("%.2f", aov_table$ges), "."
    )
    omnibus_sentences <- rbind(omnibus_sentences, data.frame(
      Measure = label, Sentence = omnibus_sentence, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))

    posthoc_test_type <- "t"

  } else {

    ## Friedman route -------------------------------------------------------
    friedman_res <- friedman_test(df, Score ~ Timepoint | ID)
    kendalls_w   <- friedman_effsize(df, Score ~ Timepoint | ID)

    omnibus_p <- friedman_res$p
    p_display <- format_p(omnibus_p)

    omnibus_summary <- rbind(omnibus_summary, data.frame(
      Measure        = label,
      Test           = "Friedman",
      N              = n_pairs,
      Direction      = direction,
      Statistic      = round(friedman_res$statistic, 3),
      Statistic_Type = "chi-sq",
      DFn            = friedman_res$df,
      DFd            = NA,
      Effect_Size    = round(kendalls_w$effsize, 3),
      Effect_Type    = "Kendall's W",
      P_Value        = p_display,
      Sphericity_Correction = "N/A (non-parametric)",
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))

    sig_clause <- if (omnibus_p < 0.05) {
      "showed a significant difference in"
    } else {
      "did not show a significant difference in"
    }
    omnibus_sentence <- paste0(
      "A Friedman test ", sig_clause, " ", label, " across the three timepoints, ",
      "\u03c7\u00b2(", friedman_res$df, ") = ", sprintf("%.2f", friedman_res$statistic),
      ", ", apa_p_clause(p_display), ", Kendall's W = ", sprintf("%.2f", kendalls_w$effsize), "."
    )
    omnibus_sentences <- rbind(omnibus_sentences, data.frame(
      Measure = label, Sentence = omnibus_sentence, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))

    posthoc_test_type <- "V"
  }

  # Post-hoc comparisons only run if THIS measure's own omnibus test was
  # significant (raw p < .05, unadjusted; the omnibus tests are not corrected
  # against each other). This gates whether the post-hoc test is computed at all,
  # and is not a filter applied afterwards.
  if (omnibus_p < 0.05) {

    if (posthoc_test_type == "t") {
      posthoc_res <- pairwise_t_test(df, Score ~ Timepoint, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "none")
    } else {
      posthoc_res <- wilcox_test(df, Score ~ Timepoint, paired = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "none")
    }

    for (i in seq_len(nrow(posthoc_res))) {
      g1 <- posthoc_res$group1[i]
      g2 <- posthoc_res$group2[i]

      mean1 <- group_means$Mean[group_means$Timepoint == g1]
      mean2 <- group_means$Mean[group_means$Timepoint == g2]

      # Matched pairs for this specific comparison — used below for
      # Mean_Diff/SE and medians regardless of route, and for the
      # effect size (Cohen's d or rank-biserial r) either way. Computed
      # once per comparison rather than per route, since both need it.
      valid_pairs <- df_wide |> filter(!is.na(.data[[g1]]), !is.na(.data[[g2]]))
      diff_vals   <- valid_pairs[[g2]] - valid_pairs[[g1]]
      mean_diff   <- mean(diff_vals)
      se_diff     <- sd(diff_vals) / sqrt(length(diff_vals))
      median1     <- median(valid_pairs[[g1]])
      median2     <- median(valid_pairs[[g2]])

      # How many of this specific comparison's complete pairs had g2 - g1 = 0
      # exactly, which are the pairs a Wilcoxon-route row's test drops before ranking.
      # Same logic as the two-timepoint route's N_Zero_Change, computed here per
      # pairwise comparison and not per measure, since each comparison has its own
      # diff_vals via valid_pairs (a participant can tie at zero on TP1-vs-TP4 but
      # not on TP1-vs-TP5, or vice versa).
      n_zero_diff_ph <- sum(diff_vals == 0)

      p_raw <- posthoc_res$p[i]

      # Effect_Size/Effect_Type alone carry whichever effect size is formally
      # correct for this row's test, with no separate always-populated Cohen's d
      # column, matching the two-timepoint route's convention.
      if (posthoc_test_type == "t") {
        # effectsize::cohens_d(), later-first ordering (g2, g1), matches this
        # pipeline's "later minus earlier" sign convention (Mean_Diff above,
        # rank_biserial below). rstatix::cohens_d(df, Score ~ Timepoint, paired = TRUE)
        # signs its effect as group1 minus group2 (earlier minus later), the opposite
        # convention, which would give a negative d next to a positive Mean_Diff on a
        # measure that increased over time.
        d_res_row <- as.data.frame(cohens_d(valid_pairs[[g2]], valid_pairs[[g1]], paired = TRUE, ci = NULL))
        effect_size_ph <- d_res_row$Cohens_d
        effect_type_ph <- "d"
      } else {
      # Rank-biserial r via effectsize::rank_biserial() on the matched pairs for this
      # specific comparison, as in the two-timepoint route. Later-timepoint-first
      # ordering (g2, g1) matches this pipeline's "later minus earlier" sign
      # convention.
      rb_res <- as.data.frame(rank_biserial(valid_pairs[[g2]], valid_pairs[[g1]], paired = TRUE, ci = NULL))
      effect_size_ph <- rb_res$r_rank_biserial
      effect_type_ph <- "r"
      }

      posthoc_summary <- rbind(posthoc_summary, data.frame(
        Measure       = label,
        Comparison    = paste0(tp_labels[g1], " vs ", tp_labels[g2]),
        N             = n_pairs,
        N_Zero_Change = n_zero_diff_ph,
        Direction     = direction,
        Mean_Group1   = round(mean1, 3),
        Mean_Group2   = round(mean2, 3),
        Median_Group1 = round(median1, 3),
        Median_Group2 = round(median2, 3),
        Mean_Diff     = round(mean_diff, 3),
        SE            = round(se_diff, 3),
        Statistic     = round(posthoc_res$statistic[i], 3),
        Statistic_Type = posthoc_test_type,
        Effect_Size   = round(effect_size_ph, 3),
        Effect_Type   = effect_type_ph,
        P_Value_Raw   = p_raw,
        Group1        = g1,
        Group2        = g2,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ))
    }
  }
}

# Bonferroni correction, run once after the full measure loop finishes, because
# it needs every member's raw p-value gathered together. The correction runs per
# hypothesis group (Mental health, Wellbeing, Behaviour, Workplace performance),
# and each group's family combines the two-timepoint tests from Part 2 with the
# post-hoc comparisons here (see the callout below this chunk). Family size
# depends on how many omnibus tests were significant.
# Days Surfing per Month and Intention to Leave are exploratory: in no group,
# never corrected (their "corrected" p-value is simply their raw p-value).
# P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric is kept alongside the formatted display column for
# the sentence generator below, which needs to test significance (< .05) without
# re-parsing a formatted string like "< 0.001" back into a number.

if (nrow(posthoc_summary) == 0) {
  print("No measure had a significant omnibus test — no post-hoc comparisons were run.")
}

# Which hypothesis group each row belongs to (NA = exploratory).
two_tp_family <- measure_family(two_tp_test_summary$Measure)
posthoc_family <- measure_family(posthoc_summary$Measure)

# One pool of every raw p-value that could be corrected, tagged with its group.
# Row order is kept, so results can be written back in the same order.
correction_pool <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Source = "two_tp",  Family = two_tp_family,  P_Raw = two_tp_test_summary$P_Value_Raw),
  tibble(Source = "posthoc", Family = posthoc_family, P_Raw = posthoc_summary$P_Value_Raw)
) |>
  mutate(
    Family_N_Tests = n(),
    P_Adjusted     = p.adjust(P_Raw, method = "bonferroni"),
    .by = Family
  ) |>
  mutate(
    # Exploratory rows (Family is NA) are not corrected.
    Family_N_Tests = if_else(is.na(Family), NA_integer_, Family_N_Tests),
    P_Adjusted     = if_else(is.na(Family), P_Raw, P_Adjusted)
  )

two_tp_pool  <- correction_pool |> filter(Source == "two_tp")
posthoc_pool <- correction_pool |> filter(Source == "posthoc")

# Label shown in the tables. Kept separate from the NA used above so the
# exploratory measures are not accidentally corrected together as a group.
label_family <- function(family) if_else(is.na(family), "Exploratory (uncorrected)", family)

# Two-timepoint tests: corrected p-value (numeric and formatted), then family.
# format_p_two_tp() keeps the no-space "<0.001" that stage 6 checks for.
two_tp_test_summary$P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric <- two_tp_pool$P_Adjusted
two_tp_test_summary$Correction_Family          <- label_family(two_tp_family)
two_tp_test_summary$Family_N_Tests             <- two_tp_pool$Family_N_Tests
two_tp_test_summary$P_Value_Bonferroni         <- as.character(format_p_two_tp(two_tp_test_summary$P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric))
two_tp_test_summary$P_Value_Raw                <- as.character(format_p_two_tp(two_tp_test_summary$P_Value_Raw))

# Post-hoc comparisons: same again. P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric stays numeric
# for the sentence generator below and for stage 6's significance brackets.
posthoc_summary$P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric <- posthoc_pool$P_Adjusted
posthoc_summary$Correction_Family          <- label_family(posthoc_family)
posthoc_summary$Family_N_Tests             <- posthoc_pool$Family_N_Tests
posthoc_summary$P_Value_Bonferroni         <- as.character(format_p(posthoc_summary$P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric))
posthoc_summary$P_Value_Raw                <- as.character(format_p(posthoc_summary$P_Value_Raw))

# One row per hypothesis group: how many tests ended up in its family, and the
# resulting Bonferroni threshold (.05 divided by that number).
correction_family_summary <- tibble(Family = family_order) |>
  left_join(
    correction_pool |>
      filter(!is.na(Family)) |>
      summarise(
        N_Tests         = n(),
        N_Two_Timepoint = sum(Source == "two_tp"),
        N_PostHoc       = sum(Source == "posthoc"),
        .by = Family
      ),
    by = "Family"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(starts_with("N_"), ~ coalesce(.x, 0L)),
    Bonferroni_Threshold = if_else(N_Tests > 0, round(0.05 / N_Tests, 4), NA_real_)
  )

cat("=== Correction families (one per hypothesis group) ===\n")
print(correction_family_summary)

# Post-hoc sentences, built after the correction above (not inside the main
# loop), since they need the Bonferroni-adjusted p-value, which does not exist
# until every significant measure's raw p-values have been gathered. There is no
# evaluative language ("indicating improvement" etc.), because that is a
# judgement about clinical meaning and not a statistical fact. Direction stays as
# its own column in the numeric tables for that purpose.
build_ttest_sentence <- function(row) {
  sig <- row$P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric < 0.05
  direction_word <- if (row$Mean_Diff > 0) "increased" else if (row$Mean_Diff < 0) "decreased" else "did not change"
  if (sig) {
    paste0(
      row$Measure, " scores significantly ", direction_word, " from ", tp_labels[row$Group1],
      " to ", tp_labels[row$Group2], " (Mdiff = ", sprintf("%.2f", row$Mean_Diff), ", SE = ",
      sprintf("%.2f", row$SE), ", ", apa_p_clause(row$P_Value_Bonferroni), ", d = ",
      sprintf("%.2f", row$Effect_Size), ")."
    )
  } else {
    paste0(
      "The difference in ", row$Measure, " scores between ", tp_labels[row$Group1], " and ",
      tp_labels[row$Group2], " was not statistically significant (Mdiff = ",
      sprintf("%.2f", row$Mean_Diff), ", SE = ", sprintf("%.2f", row$SE), ", ",
      apa_p_clause(row$P_Value_Bonferroni), ", d = ", sprintf("%.2f", row$Effect_Size), ")."
    )
  }
}

build_wilcoxon_sentence <- function(row) {
  sig <- row$P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric < 0.05

  # Names whichever timepoint actually has the higher median, rather than
  # always reporting group2-vs-group1 in a fixed order, so the sentence reads
  # naturally ("X was significantly higher than Y") whichever timepoint is listed
  # first.
  if (row$Median_Group2 > row$Median_Group1) {
    higher_label <- tp_labels[row$Group2]; higher_val <- row$Median_Group2
    lower_label  <- tp_labels[row$Group1]; lower_val  <- row$Median_Group1
  } else if (row$Median_Group1 > row$Median_Group2) {
    higher_label <- tp_labels[row$Group1]; higher_val <- row$Median_Group1
    lower_label  <- tp_labels[row$Group2]; lower_val  <- row$Median_Group2
  } else {
    higher_label <- NA; lower_label <- NA
  }

  if (sig && !is.na(higher_label)) {
    paste0(
      row$Measure, " scores were significantly higher at ", higher_label, " (Mdn = ",
      sprintf("%.2f", higher_val), ") than at ", lower_label, " (Mdn = ", sprintf("%.2f", lower_val),
      "), ", apa_p_clause(row$P_Value_Bonferroni), "."
    )
  } else {
    paste0(
      "The difference in ", row$Measure, " scores between ", tp_labels[row$Group1], " and ",
      tp_labels[row$Group2], " was not statistically significant, ",
      apa_p_clause(row$P_Value_Bonferroni), "."
    )
  }
}

posthoc_sentences <- data.frame(
  Measure    = character(),
  Comparison = character(),
  Sentence   = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

if (nrow(posthoc_summary) > 0) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(posthoc_summary))) {
    row <- posthoc_summary[i, ]
    sentence <- if (row$Statistic_Type == "t") build_ttest_sentence(row) else build_wilcoxon_sentence(row)
    # Exploratory measures are not corrected, so say so in the sentence itself.
    if (row$Correction_Family == "Exploratory (uncorrected)") {
      sentence <- paste(sentence, "(Exploratory measure; p-value not corrected for multiple testing.)")
    }
    posthoc_sentences <- rbind(posthoc_sentences, data.frame(
      Measure = row$Measure, Comparison = row$Comparison, Sentence = sentence, stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

# Four route-specific numeric tables: a display split of the computed tables
# (see callout below). The Wilcoxon table reports medians and the t-test table
# adds Mean_Diff and SE, matching what is reportable for each test type: a
# rank-based test's central tendency is its median, and a paired t-test reports
# the mean difference and its standard error as well as each group's mean.
omnibus_rmanova <- omnibus_summary |>
  filter(Test == "RM-ANOVA") |>
  select(Measure, N, Direction, F = Statistic, DFn, DFd, ges = Effect_Size,
         P_Value, Sphericity_Correction)

omnibus_friedman <- omnibus_summary |>
  filter(Test == "Friedman") |>
  select(Measure, N, Direction, Chi_Sq = Statistic, DF = DFn,
         Kendalls_W = Effect_Size, P_Value)

posthoc_ttest <- posthoc_summary |>
  filter(Statistic_Type == "t") |>
  select(Measure, Comparison, N, Direction, Mean_Group1, Mean_Group2, Mean_Diff, SE,
         t = Statistic, Cohens_d = Effect_Size, P_Value_Raw, P_Value_Bonferroni,
         Correction_Family, Family_N_Tests)

posthoc_wilcoxon <- posthoc_summary |>
  filter(Statistic_Type == "V") |>
  select(Measure, Comparison, N, N_Zero_Change, Direction, Median_Group1, Median_Group2,
         V = Statistic, Rank_Biserial_r = Effect_Size, P_Value_Raw, P_Value_Bonferroni,
         Correction_Family, Family_N_Tests)

# Two-timepoint split tables, built here because they need the corrected
# p-values calculated above. Columns are the same as the Part 2 summary, plus
# Correction_Family and Family_N_Tests at the end.
two_tp_ttest <- two_tp_test_summary |>
  filter(Statistic_Type == "t") |>
  select(Measure, N, Direction, Decision_Basis,
         Mean_TP1, SD_TP1, Mean_TP5, SD_TP5, Mean_Difference, SEM,
         DF, Mean_Diff_CI_Lower, Mean_Diff_CI_Upper,
         t = Statistic, Cohens_d = Effect_Size,
         P_Value_Raw, P_Value_Bonferroni,
         Correction_Family, Family_N_Tests)

two_tp_wilcoxon <- two_tp_test_summary |>
  filter(Statistic_Type == "W") |>
  select(Measure, N, N_Zero_Change, Direction, Decision_Basis,
         Median_TP1, Median_TP5,
         V = Statistic, Rank_Biserial_r = Effect_Size,
         P_Value_Raw, P_Value_Bonferroni,
         Correction_Family, Family_N_Tests)

# Sorted by domain for display, after the correction by hypothesis group has
# been applied above. omnibus_summary, posthoc_summary and two_tp_test_summary
# stay in their original order.
two_tp_ttest      <- sort_by_domain(two_tp_ttest, "Measure")
two_tp_wilcoxon   <- sort_by_domain(two_tp_wilcoxon, "Measure")
omnibus_rmanova   <- sort_by_domain(omnibus_rmanova, "Measure")
omnibus_friedman  <- sort_by_domain(omnibus_friedman, "Measure")
posthoc_ttest     <- sort_by_domain(posthoc_ttest, "Measure")
posthoc_wilcoxon  <- sort_by_domain(posthoc_wilcoxon, "Measure")
omnibus_sentences <- sort_by_domain(omnibus_sentences, "Measure")
posthoc_sentences <- sort_by_domain(posthoc_sentences, "Measure")

cat("=== Two-timepoint: paired t-tests ===\n")
print(two_tp_ttest)
cat("\n=== Two-timepoint: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests ===\n")
print(two_tp_wilcoxon)
cat("\n=== RM-ANOVA omnibus tests ===\n")
print(omnibus_rmanova)
cat("\n=== Friedman omnibus tests ===\n")
print(omnibus_friedman)
cat("\n=== Post-hoc: paired t-tests ===\n")
print(posthoc_ttest)
cat("\n=== Post-hoc: Wilcoxon signed-rank tests ===\n")
print(posthoc_wilcoxon)
cat("\n=== APA-style sentences: omnibus tests ===\n")
print(omnibus_sentences)
cat("\n=== APA-style sentences: post-hoc comparisons ===\n")
print(posthoc_sentences)
```

::: callout-important
**Bonferroni correction runs per hypothesis group.**

Each Hypothesis 1 group (Mental health, Wellbeing, Behaviour, Workplace performance; defined in the measure lookup, stage 4c) is one family. A family holds that group's two-timepoint tests (Part 2) plus every post-hoc comparison run for its three-timepoint measures, including the 2-week vs 3-month comparison, which is not hypothesised but is corrected with the rest. Omnibus tests are not corrected. Family size depends on how many omnibus tests were significant. `correction_family_summary` shows each family's actual size and threshold (.05 divided by its size).

**Exploratory measures are not corrected.** Days Surfing per Month and Intention to Leave are in no group (`Correction_Family` = "Exploratory (uncorrected)"). For them `P_Value_Bonferroni` and `P_Value_Bonferroni_Numeric` equal the raw p-value. The columns are kept, and not left blank, so stage 6 can read them without failing. The post-hoc sentence for an exploratory measure says so.

The two-timepoint split tables (`two_tp_ttest`, `two_tp_wilcoxon`) are built in the chunk above, after the correction. All four split tables, `two_tp_test_summary` and `posthoc_summary` carry `Correction_Family` and `Family_N_Tests`. `omnibus_summary` does not.
:::

::: callout-note
**Post-hoc gating.** Post-hoc comparisons run for a measure only if its own omnibus test was significant (raw, unadjusted p \< .05). The omnibus tests are not corrected against each other. If no measure reaches significance, `posthoc_summary` stays empty and a message says so.

**Correction.** The pairwise calls use `p.adjust.method = "none"` to return raw p-values, which are collected in `P_Value_Raw` across the loop. The Bonferroni correction is then applied once, after the loop, within each hypothesis group (see the callout above), so family size is not fixed in advance.

**Split tables.** `omnibus_rmanova`, `omnibus_friedman`, `posthoc_ttest` and `posthoc_wilcoxon` are display-only copies of `omnibus_summary` and `posthoc_summary`, filtered and renamed so each table's columns read as the quantities that test reports (for example `Statistic` becomes `F` in the RM-ANOVA table and `t` in the paired-t post-hoc table). `omnibus_summary` and `posthoc_summary` are the tables saved to the workbook and passed to stage 6.

**`N_Zero_Change` in `posthoc_wilcoxon`.** As in the two-timepoint route, `wilcox_test()` ranks non-zero differences only, so `N` can overstate how many pairs drove a comparison when a measure has a floor or ceiling effect. `N_Zero_Change` is computed per pairwise comparison (`sum(diff_vals == 0)` on that comparison's own `valid_pairs`), because a participant can tie at zero for one pair of timepoints and not another. It is shown only in `posthoc_wilcoxon`, since a paired t-test does not drop zero-difference pairs.

**Known limitation on `N`.** In `posthoc_summary` and its split tables, `N` is `n_pairs`, computed once per measure as `n_distinct(df$ID)`. It is not recalculated per comparison. If a measure has uneven missingness across timepoints, a comparison's complete-case count could differ from the `N` shown on its row, and `N` and `N_Zero_Change` on the same row would then not be strictly comparable.

**Sentence tables.** `omnibus_sentences` and `posthoc_sentences` give one ready-to-paste APA-style sentence per row, kept separate from the numeric tables so those stay easy to scan. Generalised eta-squared (`ges`) is reported throughout and not partial eta-squared. Post-hoc sentences state which timepoint was higher and which way the mean moved, without saying whether that direction is good or bad. `Direction` stays as its own column for that purpose.
:::

**Cohen's *d* sign.** `rstatix::cohens_d(df, Score ~ Timepoint, paired = TRUE)` signs its effect as group1 minus group2 (earlier minus later), whereas `Mean_Diff` and the rank-biserial *r* use this pipeline's later-minus-earlier convention. Cohen's *d* is therefore computed with `effectsize::cohens_d()` on the matched pairs for each specific comparison, later-first, so its sign matches `Mean_Diff`.

## Part 4 — RCI (Reliable Change Index)

Jacobson-Truax classification: calculation and classification only. The scatter plots are in stage 6. This covers 17 targets (see the introduction to this stage for the exceptions: GSPA and HPQ Presenteeism take sourced reliability values, and INTL and HPQ Absenteeism are excluded). Cutoffs, directions and column names are set in the `rci_targets` table below. Reliability values are computed live from TP1 data, except where a sourced value is stated.

::: callout-note
**Reference figures in `rci_summary`.** For every measure and comparison row the table reports `SD_Pre`, `SEM`, `S_Diff`, `Z_Critical`, `CI_Level` and `RC_Required`, so a reliable-change calculation can be reported in full (for example "reliable change required was at least X points (Sdiff = Y; 95% CI, z = 1.96)"). `jt_classify()` calculates them once, using the same complete-pairs sample and formula as `cs_distribution()`, and attaches them to its return value as `attr(df, "rci_stats")`. A single `rci_significance_level` constant is passed to `cs_distribution()` explicitly, so the value driving the classification and the value reported cannot drift apart.

**Counts.** `rci_summary` also reports `N_Recovered`, `N_Improved`, `N_Unchanged`, `N_Deteriorated` and `N_Harmed`, each placed before its matching `Pct_*` column, for "*n* (%)" reporting. They come from `jt_counts$n` through `get_n()`, which mirrors `get_pct()`. The five counts sum to that row's `N`.
:::

### RCI classification functions

```{r}
#| label: s05-rci-functions
# General-purpose RCI classifier: numeric cutoff (or no cutoff), five-category
# classification (Recovered/Improved/Unchanged/Deteriorated/Harmed) matching
# clinicalsignificance::cs_combined()'s own scheme (Claus et al., JSS,
# <doi:10.18637/jss.v111.i01>).
#
# The RCI calculation runs through cs_distribution(). Its JT method computes
# se_measurement = sd_pre * sqrt(1 - reliability) and
# s_diff = sqrt(2 * se_measurement^2).
#
# The clinical cutoff comparison is NOT delegated to the package. cs_combined()
# only computes its OWN cutoff from population statistics (its cutoff_type
# "a"/"b"/"c" formulas) and cannot accept an externally sourced, already
# published cutoff value. Most of this project's cutoffs (SWEMWBS, PHQ-8, GAD-7,
# GSPA) are specific published clinical cutoffs from each instrument's own
# literature, so the cutoff-crossing comparison below is this project's own
# code, combined with cs_distribution()'s reliable-change category the way
# cs_combined() combines the two internally.
#
# The five-category scheme is fully symmetric: Recovered pairs with Harmed
# (both involve crossing the cutoff), and Improved pairs with Deteriorated (both
# stay on the same side), matching cs_combined()'s own category definitions.
# Someone who starts below the cutoff and reliably gets worse is therefore
# classed as Deteriorated and does not fall through to "Unchanged".
jt_classify <- function(data, id_col, pre_col, post_col,
                         cutoff = NULL, reliability,
                         direction = c("positive", "negative"),
                         significance_level = 0.05) {

  direction <- match.arg(direction)
  better_is <- if (direction == "positive") "higher" else "lower"

  df <- data |>
    select({{id_col}}, {{pre_col}}, {{post_col}}) |>
    rename(id = {{id_col}}, score_pre = {{pre_col}}, score_post = {{post_col}}) |>
    filter(!is.na(score_pre), !is.na(score_post))

  # Reliable-change reference figures for reporting: SD at baseline, standard error
  # of measurement (SEM), standard error of the difference (S_diff), the critical z
  # for the chosen significance level, and the raw-score change required to count
  # as reliable (RC_required = z * S_diff). Computed once here, from the same
  # complete-pairs sample the classification below uses, with the identical
  # formula cs_distribution() applies internally. This is not a second,
  # separately maintained calculation. It keeps numbers the classification
  # already depends on, so they do not have to be worked out again wherever they
  # are needed for output.
  sd_pre      <- sd(df$score_pre, na.rm = TRUE)
  sem         <- sd_pre * sqrt(1 - reliability)
  s_diff      <- sqrt(2 * sem^2)
  z_critical  <- qnorm(1 - significance_level / 2)
  rc_required <- z_critical * s_diff

  # cs_distribution() needs long format: one row per participant per
  # timepoint, not one row per participant with separate pre/post columns.
  df_long <- df |>
    pivot_longer(cols = c(score_pre, score_post), names_to = "time_label", values_to = "outcome") |>
    mutate(time = if_else(time_label == "score_pre", 1, 2)) |>
    select(id, time, outcome)

  cs_res <- cs_distribution(
    df_long, id = id, time = time, outcome = outcome,
    pre = 1, post = 2, reliability = reliability,
    better_is = better_is, rci_method = "JT",
    significance_level = significance_level
  )

  rci_out <- cs_get_augmented_data(cs_res) |>
    select(id, rci, cs_category = category)

  df <- df |>
    left_join(rci_out, by = "id") |>
    rename(RCI = rci)

  if (!is.null(cutoff)) {

    if (direction == "positive") {
      df <- df |>
        mutate(
          status_pre  = ifelse(score_pre  >= cutoff, "Functional", "Dysfunctional"),
          status_post = ifelse(score_post >= cutoff, "Functional", "Dysfunctional")
        )
    } else {
      df <- df |>
        mutate(
          status_pre  = ifelse(score_pre  >= cutoff, "Dysfunctional", "Functional"),
          status_post = ifelse(score_post >= cutoff, "Dysfunctional", "Functional")
        )
    }

    df <- df |>
      mutate(
        JT_raw = case_when(
          cs_category == "Improved" & status_pre == "Dysfunctional" & status_post == "Functional" ~ "Recovered",
          cs_category == "Improved" ~ "Improved",
          cs_category == "Deteriorated" & status_pre == "Functional" & status_post == "Dysfunctional" ~ "Harmed",
          cs_category == "Deteriorated" ~ "Deteriorated",
          TRUE ~ "Unchanged"
        )
      )

  } else {
    df <- df |> mutate(JT_raw = as.character(cs_category))
  }

  # Attached as an attribute, not a new column — so it rides along with the
  # classified data without count(JT_raw)/summarise_jt() needing to know to
  # ignore it. Set here, as the last step before df is returned, since
  # select()/filter()/mutate()/left_join() above all preserve attributes,
  # but that's only guaranteed for code that stays exactly this shape — if
  # this function's internals are reordered later, re-check that the
  # attribute still survives through to what's returned.
  attr(df, "rci_stats") <- list(
    SD_Pre      = sd_pre,
    SEM         = sem,
    S_Diff      = s_diff,
    Z_Critical  = z_critical,
    CI_Level    = paste0(100 * (1 - significance_level), "%"),
    RC_Required = rc_required
  )

  df
}

# ITQ PTSD/DSO/CPTSD Totals run through jt_classify() above like every other
# target, with no separate ITQ classifier (see the callout below the RCI target
# list).
```

### Cronbach's alpha, calculated from TP1 item data

This computes Cronbach's alpha directly from the baseline (TP1) data, one alpha per RCI target, using item groupings that match each RCI target exactly (e.g. BAT Cognitive Impairment's alpha comes only from its own 3 items, not the full 12-item BAT). The reliability estimate stays live and reflects the actual sample if the data changes.

::: callout-note
**Two exceptions to computed alpha.**

- **GSPA** has no computed alpha. Its three components (strenuous, moderate and mild session counts) are combined by a fixed weighted formula into a composite index and are not interchangeable indicators of one construct, so Cronbach's alpha is not the right concept. Reliability is set to **0.74**, the lower-bound ICC in GSPA validation studies, chosen as the more conservative published estimate.
- **INTL is not in the RCI.** A 2-item, self-made, unvalidated measure gives an unstable alpha with no external literature to check it against. INTL gets a simple scatter plot instead (stage 6).

Cronbach's alpha is computed by hand, because the formula is standard and unambiguous, so no extra package is needed.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-cronbachs-alpha-function
cronbachs_alpha <- function(item_data) {
  item_data <- item_data[complete.cases(item_data), ]
  k <- ncol(item_data)
  item_variances <- sapply(item_data, stats::var)
  total_score    <- rowSums(item_data)
  total_variance <- stats::var(total_score)

  alpha <- (k / (k - 1)) * (1 - sum(item_variances) / total_variance)
  round(alpha, 3)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: s05-rci-item-groupings
# Item groupings, matched exactly to each RCI target's own scoring — pulled
# directly from the column patterns used in stage 4a.
rci_item_groups <- list(
  "SWEMWBS"                  = paste0("SWEMWBS_", 1:7, "_TP1"),
  "PHQ-8"                    = paste0("PHQ8_", 1:8, "_TP1"),
  "GAD-7"                    = paste0("GAD7_", 1:7, "_TP1"),
  "ITQ PTSD"                 = paste0("ITQ_P", 1:6, "_TP1"),
  "ITQ DSO"                  = paste0("ITQ_C", 1:6, "_TP1"),
  "ITQ CPTSD"                = c(paste0("ITQ_P", 1:6, "_TP1"), paste0("ITQ_C", 1:6, "_TP1")),
  "MHSIS"                    = paste0("MHSIS_", 1:3, "_TP1"),
  "BRS"                      = paste0("BRS_", 1:6, "_TP1"),
  "UWES"                     = paste0("UWES_", 1:3, "_TP1"),
  "OSES"                     = paste0("OSES_", 1:6, "_TP1"),
  "BAT Total"                = paste0("BAT_", 1:12, "_TP1"),
  "BAT Exhaustion"           = paste0("BAT_", 1:3, "_TP1"),
  "BAT Mental Distance"      = paste0("BAT_", 4:6, "_TP1"),
  "BAT Emotional Impairment" = paste0("BAT_", 7:9, "_TP1"),
  "BAT Cognitive Impairment" = paste0("BAT_", 10:12, "_TP1")
)

rci_computed_alpha <- map_dfr(names(rci_item_groups), function(label) {
  tibble(
    Label       = label,
    Reliability = cronbachs_alpha(scored_data[rci_item_groups[[label]]])
  )
})

print(rci_computed_alpha)
```

### RCI target list

Cutoffs, directions and TP1/TP4/TP5 column names are set in this table. Reliability values come from `rci_computed_alpha` above (joined by `Label`), except GSPA and HPQ Presenteeism, which are set directly to their sourced values.

::: callout-note
**ITQ totals.** ITQ PTSD, DSO and CPTSD Totals run through the same `jt_classify()` as every other target, on the continuous total score with no diagnostic-category logic. `Cutoff` is `NA` for all three, because none has a published RCI-appropriate clinical cutoff, so they produce only Improved, Deteriorated or Unchanged and never Recovered or Harmed. `Direction` is "negative" (higher score = worse). `TP4Col` is `NA`, because ITQ is not administered at TP4, so the loop skips the TP1-vs-TP4 comparison and these targets run TP1 vs TP5 only. ITQ CPTSD reliability comes from the "ITQ CPTSD" entry in `rci_item_groups` (all 12 ITQ items); ITQ PTSD and ITQ DSO use their own 6-item groupings.

**HPQ Presenteeism** runs through `jt_classify()` with `Cutoff` `NA`, `Direction` "positive" (higher percentage = better performance) and `TP4Col` `NA_character_`, because HPQ is not administered at TP4. It is not a multi-item scale, so it has no `rci_item_groups` entry and no computed alpha. Reliability is set to **0.89**, the test-retest ICC for the HPQ presenteeism scale in Kessler et al. (2004, *n* = 551).

**HPQ Absenteeism is excluded from the RCI.** Published reliability estimates for the 4-week absenteeism-hours item are inconsistent (ICC 0.471 to 0.814 depending on sample), and no single value is defensible for a population close to this study's (UK emergency service workers). GSPA and HPQ Presenteeism use sourced reliability values, and INTL is excluded, on the same logic.
:::

```{r}
#| label: s05-rci-target-list
rci_targets <- tribble(
  ~Label,                      ~PreCol,                    ~TP4Col,                    ~TP5Col,                    ~Cutoff, ~Direction,  ~Type,
  "SWEMWBS",                   "SWEMWBS_Metric_TP1",       "SWEMWBS_Metric_TP4",       "SWEMWBS_Metric_TP5",       19.3,    "positive",  "standard",
  "PHQ-8",                     "PHQ8_Total_TP1",           "PHQ8_Total_TP4",           "PHQ8_Total_TP5",           10,      "negative",  "standard",
  "GAD-7",                     "GAD7_Total_TP1",           "GAD7_Total_TP4",           "GAD7_Total_TP5",           8,      "negative",  "standard",
  "MHSIS",                     "MHSIS_Mean_TP1",           "MHSIS_Mean_TP4",           "MHSIS_Mean_TP5",           NA,      "positive",  "standard",
  "BRS",                       "BRS_Mean_TP1",             "BRS_Mean_TP4",             "BRS_Mean_TP5",             NA,      "positive",  "standard",
  "UWES",                      "UWES_Total_TP1",           "UWES_Total_TP4",           "UWES_Total_TP5",           NA,      "positive",  "standard",
  "OSES",                      "OSES_Total_TP1",           "OSES_Total_TP4",           "OSES_Total_TP5",           NA,      "positive",  "standard",
  "BAT Total",                 "BAT_TotalMean_TP1",        "BAT_TotalMean_TP4",        "BAT_TotalMean_TP5",        NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "BAT Exhaustion",            "BAT_Exhaustion_TP1",       "BAT_Exhaustion_TP4",       "BAT_Exhaustion_TP5",       NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "BAT Mental Distance",       "BAT_MentalDistance_TP1",   "BAT_MentalDistance_TP4",   "BAT_MentalDistance_TP5",   NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "BAT Emotional Impairment",  "BAT_EmoImpairment_TP1",    "BAT_EmoImpairment_TP4",    "BAT_EmoImpairment_TP5",    NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "BAT Cognitive Impairment",  "BAT_CogImpairment_TP1",    "BAT_CogImpairment_TP4",    "BAT_CogImpairment_TP5",    NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "GSPA",                      "GSPA_Total_TP1",           "GSPA_Total_TP4",           "GSPA_Total_TP5",           24,      "positive",  "standard",
  "ITQ PTSD",                  "ITQ_PTSD_Total_TP1",       NA_character_,              "ITQ_PTSD_Total_TP5",       NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "ITQ DSO",                   "ITQ_DSO_Total_TP1",        NA_character_,              "ITQ_DSO_Total_TP5",        NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "ITQ CPTSD",                 "ITQ_CPTSD_Total_TP1",      NA_character_,              "ITQ_CPTSD_Total_TP5",      NA,      "negative",  "standard",
  "HPQ Presenteeism",          "HPQ_presenteeism_percent_TP1", NA_character_,          "HPQ_presenteeism_percent_TP5", NA,  "positive",  "standard"
) |>
  left_join(rci_computed_alpha, by = "Label") |>
  mutate(Reliability = case_when(
    Label == "GSPA"             ~ 0.74,
    Label == "HPQ Presenteeism" ~ 0.89,
    TRUE                        ~ Reliability
  ))

print(rci_targets)
```

### Run RCI for all targets

```{r}
#| label: s05-rci-run-standard
# 95% CI, two-tailed — Jacobson & Truax (1991) convention. Set once here and
# passed into jt_classify() below, rather than relying on cs_distribution()'s
# own default (which is also 0.05, so this changes nothing about the
# classification itself — it just makes the value visible in the script
# instead of implicit, and ties the z reported in rci_summary to the exact
# value the classification actually used).
rci_significance_level <- 0.05

rci_results <- list()
rci_summary <- data.frame(
  Measure       = character(),
  Comparison    = character(),
  N             = numeric(),
  Reliability   = numeric(),
  SD_Pre        = numeric(),
  SEM           = numeric(),
  S_Diff        = numeric(),
  Z_Critical    = numeric(),
  CI_Level      = character(),
  RC_Required   = numeric(),
  N_Recovered   = numeric(),
  Pct_Recovered = numeric(),
  N_Improved    = numeric(),
  Pct_Improved  = numeric(),
  N_Unchanged   = numeric(),
  Pct_Unchanged = numeric(),
  N_Deteriorated = numeric(),
  Pct_Deteriorated = numeric(),
  N_Harmed      = numeric(),
  Pct_Harmed    = numeric(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

summarise_jt <- function(df) {
  df |>
    count(JT_raw) |>
    mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1))
}

for (i in seq_len(nrow(rci_targets))) {

  label       <- rci_targets$Label[i]
  pre_col     <- rci_targets$PreCol[i]
  tp4_col     <- rci_targets$TP4Col[i]
  tp5_col     <- rci_targets$TP5Col[i]
  cutoff      <- if (is.na(rci_targets$Cutoff[i])) NULL else rci_targets$Cutoff[i]
  reliability <- rci_targets$Reliability[i]
  direction   <- rci_targets$Direction[i]

  for (comparison in c("TP1_vs_TP4", "TP1_vs_TP5")) {

    post_col <- if (comparison == "TP1_vs_TP4") tp4_col else tp5_col

    # Skip a comparison this target doesn't have — ITQ PTSD/DSO/CPTSD and
    # HPQ Presenteeism, which have no TP4Col since neither is administered
    # at TP4. Without this check, .data[[NA]] below would error.
    if (is.na(post_col)) next

    classified <- jt_classify(
      data = scored_data, id_col = ID,
      pre_col = .data[[pre_col]], post_col = .data[[post_col]],
      cutoff = cutoff, reliability = reliability, direction = direction,
      significance_level = rci_significance_level
    )

    # SD_Pre, SEM, S_Diff, Z_Critical, CI_Level, RC_Required — worked out
    # once inside jt_classify() itself (see the function definition above)
    # and attached to its return value, rather than recalculated here.
    rci_stats <- attr(classified, "rci_stats")

    key <- paste0(label, "__", comparison)
    rci_results[[key]] <- classified

    jt_counts <- summarise_jt(classified)

    # Exact match, not a prefix pattern: the five categories are clean, atomic
    # strings (Recovered/Improved/Unchanged/Deteriorated/Harmed), so no "^Improved"
    # regex is needed.
    get_pct <- function(category) {
      matches <- jt_counts$pct[jt_counts$JT_raw == category]
      if (length(matches) == 0) 0 else sum(matches)
    }

    # Same exact-match logic as get_pct() above, reading the raw count
    # (jt_counts$n, already produced by count(JT_raw) inside
    # summarise_jt()) rather than the percentage — so "n (%)" reporting
    # (e.g. "30 (59.3%)") can be built from these two columns together,
    # rather than only having the percentage on its own.
    get_n <- function(category) {
      matches <- jt_counts$n[jt_counts$JT_raw == category]
      if (length(matches) == 0) 0 else sum(matches)
    }

    rci_summary <- rbind(rci_summary, data.frame(
      Measure       = label,
      Comparison    = comparison,
      N             = nrow(classified),
      Reliability   = reliability,
      SD_Pre        = round(rci_stats$SD_Pre, 3),
      SEM           = round(rci_stats$SEM, 3),
      S_Diff        = round(rci_stats$S_Diff, 3),
      Z_Critical    = round(rci_stats$Z_Critical, 3),
      CI_Level      = rci_stats$CI_Level,
      RC_Required   = round(rci_stats$RC_Required, 3),
      N_Recovered   = get_n("Recovered"),
      Pct_Recovered = get_pct("Recovered"),
      N_Improved    = get_n("Improved"),
      Pct_Improved  = get_pct("Improved"),
      N_Unchanged   = get_n("Unchanged"),
      Pct_Unchanged = get_pct("Unchanged"),
      N_Deteriorated = get_n("Deteriorated"),
      Pct_Deteriorated = get_pct("Deteriorated"),
      N_Harmed      = get_n("Harmed"),
      Pct_Harmed    = get_pct("Harmed"),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

# Sorted by domain for display and export. rci_results (the classified data
# frames) is a named list and is not affected.
rci_summary <- sort_by_domain(rci_summary, "Measure")

print(rci_summary)
```
